title: Blood Culture Positivity, Microbiological Spectrum, and Inflammatory Correlates in Patients Hospitalized with SARS-CoV-2 Infection During the Omicron BA.5 Wave: A Retrospective Cohort Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to characterize blood-culture positivity, pathogen distribution, inflammatory correlates, antimicrobial exposure, and short-term outcomes in a homogeneous cohort hospitalized during the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.5 wave. Blood cultures are frequently obtained in hospitalized patients with COVID-19, although the diagnostic yield and clinical meaning of culture positivity vary markedly according to case mix, disease severity, and timing of sampling.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective observational study included 395 patients hospitalized with SARS-CoV-2 infection between 12 July and 25 September 2022. Patients were categorized as blood-culture positive when a named bacterial species was recorded and as culture negative when "No growth" was documented. Omicron-era data remain comparatively limited.
analysis.methods: Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test and categorical variables using Fisher’s exact or chi-square tests, as appropriate. A parsimonious multivariable logistic regression model was used to explore factors independently associated with blood-culture positivity.
analysis.main_results: Blood cultures were positive in 89/395 patients (22.5%). Gram-positive organisms accounted for 52.8% of positive cultures and Gram-negative organisms for 47.2%. In the adjusted model, higher leukocyte count remained independently associated with culture positivity (aOR 1.10 per 1 × 109/L, 95% CI 1.05–1.15; p < 0.001), while vaccination status showed an inverse exploratory association (aOR 0.58, 95% CI 0.35–0.96; p = 0.033).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Blood-culture positivity was common in this hospitalized BA.5 cohort and showed a nearly balanced Gram-positive/Gram-negative distribution. Leukocytosis and clinically documented sepsis were the clearest correlates of positivity, whereas mortality did not differ significantly.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support selective blood-culture use driven by bacterial infection signals and emphasize the need to connect antimicrobial decisions to microbiological evidence. A documented sepsis diagnosis was more frequent in the culture-positive group (48.3% vs. 28.1%; OR 2.39, 95% CI 1.47–3.88; p < 0.001).
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The exploratory model AUC was 0.672 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.608–0.731); calibration was not assessed. Mortality was numerically higher with culture positivity (20.2% vs. 14.4%) but did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.188).

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective cohort study analyzed blood culture positivity in 395 hospitalized patients with SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.5 infection between July and September 2022. It found that 22.5% of patients had positive blood cultures, with a nearly equal distribution of Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms. The most common isolates were Streptococcus pneumoniae, Enterococcus faecalis, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Higher leukocyte counts were independently associated with culture positivity, while vaccination status showed an inverse exploratory association. Although mortality was higher in culture-positive patients, the difference was not statistically significant. The study highlights the importance of using microbiological evidence to guide antimicrobial decisions in hospitalized patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection.

title: The platform trial in COVID-19 priming and BOOsting (PICOBOO): The reactogenicity of nine licensed COVID-19 vaccines delivered in immunocompetent adults.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the reactogenicity of nine licensed COVID-19 vaccines in immunocompetent adults, addressing the need to understand vaccine safety profiles during booster and additional dose administration.
analysis.study_design_and_population: PICOBOO is a randomised, Bayesian adaptive trial evaluating immunogenicity and reactogenicity of licensed COVID-19 vaccines in immunocompetent individuals aged >12 years. Participants were randomised within each stratum to receive a single vaccine dose. A total of 1049 COVID-19 vaccine doses were administered to 586 adults enrolled between March 2022 and September 2024.
analysis.methods: Individuals who had not received a COVID-19 vaccine within three months were eligible. Reactogenicity events were recorded on days 1-7 following vaccination. Serious or medically attended adverse events (AEs), AEs of special interest, and AEs resulting in withdrawal were collected through day 28. Participants were followed until day 720.
analysis.main_results: At least one local reaction was reported after 786 (75%) doses and at least one systemic reaction after 798 (76%) doses. Local reactogenicity ranged from 47% (110/236) with NVX-CoV2373 (Nvx) to 90% (131/145) with Moderna, while systemic reactogenicity ranged from 69% (162/236) with Nvx to 85% (121/143) with BNT162b2. Severe reactogenicity events were rare.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Reactogenicity events were common but rarely severe. Although reactogenicity appeared less frequent following Nvx than mRNA vaccines within strata, the trial was not powered for between-vaccine comparisons and findings should be interpreted descriptively.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide descriptive insights into the reactogenicity profiles of various licensed vaccines, which can inform future vaccine development and administration strategies for immunocompetent adults.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Reactogenicity events were recorded on days 1-7, and serious adverse events were collected through day 28, which may limit the assessment of long-term effects.

analysis.summary_en: This study, PICOBOO, evaluated the reactogenicity of nine licensed COVID-19 vaccines in immunocompetent adults aged over 12 years. The trial, which ran from March 2022 to September 2024, randomised participants within strata based on age and primary vaccination regimen. Reactogenicity events were recorded on days 1-7, with serious adverse events tracked through day 28. Results showed that local reactions occurred after 75% of doses, and systemic reactions after 76%. Pain was the most common local reaction, while headache, fatigue, myalgia, and chills were the most frequent systemic reactions. Severe reactogenicity events were rare. The study found that reactogenicity varied between vaccines, with mRNA vaccines showing higher rates than NVX-CoV2373. However, the trial was not powered for between-vaccine comparisons, and findings should be interpreted descriptively. These results can inform future vaccine administration strategies and safety monitoring for immunocompetent adults.
